tagline: Return a filtered table expression — CALCULATE's table-returning counterpart, used inside iterators and table functions

slides.title: CALCULATETABLE — CALCULATE for Tables
slides.body: CALCULATETABLE works exactly like CALCULATE but returns a filtered table instead of a scalar value. It applies filter arguments to a table expression and returns the rows that pass those filters. This makes it essential for creating filtered tables to pass into iterators (SUMX, COUNTROWS), relationship functions (USERELATIONSHIP), or other table-consuming DAX functions. Anywhere you need a filtered table — not just a filtered scalar — CALCULATETABLE is the answer.
slides.keyPoint: CALCULATETABLE(Table, Filter1, Filter2, ...) → returns a filtered table. CALCULATE(Expression, Filter1, ...) → returns a scalar. They share the same filter modification logic — CALCULATETABLE just targets a table instead of an expression.

slides.title: Sales Data — Full Table
slides.caption: We want to count only active customers who have placed orders over $500
slides.note: Goal: COUNTROWS of the filtered table where Status = 'Active' AND OrderAmount > 500. Result should be 2 (C001 and C003).

slides.title: CALCULATETABLE vs FILTER — Key Difference
slides.code:
-- Using CALCULATETABLE (modifies filter context — preferred)
ActiveHighValue =
COUNTROWS(
    CALCULATETABLE(
        Sales,
        Sales[Status] = "Active",
        Sales[OrderAmount] > 500
    )
)
-- Returns: 2 (C001, C003)

-- Using FILTER (iterates rows — slower on large tables)
ActiveHighValueFilter =
COUNTROWS(
    FILTER(
        Sales,
        Sales[Status] = "Active" && Sales[OrderAmount] > 500
    )
)
-- Returns: 2 (same result, different mechanism)

-- CALCULATETABLE in a security filter (RLS alternative)
DeptAccess =
CALCULATETABLE(
    Employees,
    DeptAccess[ManagerEmail] = USERPRINCIPALNAME()
)
slides.annotation: CALCULATETABLE applies filter arguments as context modifications — using the same efficient engine as CALCULATE. FILTER iterates row by row. For simple column filters, CALCULATETABLE is faster and more readable.

slides.title: Result — Filtered Table from CALCULATETABLE
slides.caption: CALCULATETABLE returns only rows matching both filter conditions
slides.note: COUNTROWS of the CALCULATETABLE result = 2. The filtered table contains only C001 and C003.

slides.title: When to Use CALCULATETABLE
bullets: Inside an iterator that needs a pre-filtered table: SUMX(CALCULATETABLE(Sales, ...), [Amount])
To create a virtual security filter table for RLS: CALCULATETABLE(Employees, AccessTable[Email] = USERPRINCIPALNAME())
When building virtual relationships using TREATAS: TREATAS(CALCULATETABLE(Budget, ...), Actuals[CostCenter])
Inside COUNTROWS when you need a filtered count: COUNTROWS(CALCULATETABLE(Orders, Orders[Status] = "Shipped"))
The key distinction: CALCULATETABLE returns a TABLE; CALCULATE returns a SCALAR — choose based on what the outer function expects
slides.keyPoint: Use CALCULATETABLE when the outer function expects a table argument and you need to apply filters to that table. CALCULATE wraps a scalar expression. Never mix them up — CALCULATE cannot be used where a table is expected.

slides.title: PL-300 Exam — Key Facts
bullets: CALCULATETABLE and CALCULATE share the same filter argument syntax and semantics — they differ only in what they return (table vs scalar)
CALCULATETABLE is frequently used in RLS expressions to filter a security bridge table

FILTER(Table, condition) is the alternative — but CALCULATETABLE is preferred for simple column filters because it is evaluated at the storage engine level (faster than FILTER's Formula Engine row iteration)
CALCULATETABLE cannot be used inside a measure's return position where a scalar is expected — it returns a table
Common exam scenario: 'A measure needs to count rows matching multiple conditions' → COUNTROWS(CALCULATETABLE(...))
slides.keyPoint: Exam shortcut: whenever a question asks for a filtered COUNT of rows, COUNTROWS(CALCULATETABLE(Table, filter1, filter2)) is almost always the cleanest answer — and one CALCULATE call with ALL the filter args is more readable than nested FILTERs.
